sections.b: Ahaz came to the throne young, in a dangerous decade. When Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel marched on Jerusalem to replace him with "the son of Tabeal" (Isaiah 7:6), Isaiah met him at the water channel of the Upper Pool and urged him to stay calm and trust the LORD: "If you will not hold firm, you will not be held firm" (Isaiah 7:9). Ahaz refused even to ask for a sign, and Isaiah gave him one anyway, the child Immanuel (Isaiah 7:10–17). Kings tells what Ahaz did instead: he sent the Temple's silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser with the message "I am your servant", copied an altar he saw in Damascus, and sacrificed his son in the fire (2 Kings 16:3–18). Tiglath-pileser's own records list him among the kings who paid tribute. Isaiah sets him against his son Hezekiah, who meets the Assyrian envoy at the same channel and trusts (Isaiah 36–37).
sections.refs: Isaiah 7:1–17; Isaiah 8:1–8; Isaiah 14:28; 2 Kings 16:1–20; 2 Chronicles 28:1–27; Isaiah 36:2

sections.h: The sign and the name in Isaiah 7–9
sections.b: The name Immanuel, "God is with us", appears three times in Isaiah. In 7:14 it is the name a young woman will give her son, a sign to the house of David that Aram and Israel will soon fall. In 8:8 the Assyrian flood covers "your land, Immanuel", so the child is the owner of Judah's land, which sounds like a king. In 8:10 it becomes a cry of faith against the nations: "for God is with us". Many readers see the same royal child again in 9:6–7 and 11:1–5. Jewish interpreters identify him with Hezekiah or a son of Isaiah; Christian readers, following Matthew 1:23, with Jesus, either directly or as the final meaning of a sign first given to Ahaz. The note on Isaiah 7:14 and the chapter page set out each view.
sections.refs: Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 8:8; Isaiah 8:10; Isaiah 9:6–7; Matthew 1:23; Matthew 28:20

sections.b: Matthew 1:23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 in the Greek: "Look, the virgin will be pregnant and will have a son, and they will give him the name Immanuel." The Hebrew has 'almah, a young woman of marriageable age, where the Greek translators of the 2nd century BC put parthenos, usually "virgin". Later translators (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) chose neanis, "young woman", and the two words became the center of the Jewish–Christian debate already recorded in Justin's Dialogue with Trypho. Christians differ on how the verse foretells Jesus' birth: as a direct prediction, or as a sign to Ahaz whose full meaning arrived in Mary's child. The faith in the virginal conception rests on Matthew and Luke; the argument over Isaiah's word concerns how Matthew read the prophet.

sections.h: The royal child and the shoot of Jesse (Isaiah 9 and 11)
sections.b: Isaiah 9:1–7 and 11:1–10 are the main messianic poems of the first part of Isaiah. The first celebrates a child "born to us" who will sit "on David's throne" with a rule of endless peace and four great names (Isaiah 9:6–7). The second pictures a shoot from "Jesse's stump" on whom the LORD's Spirit rests, who judges the poor rightly, and whose reign brings peace even to the animals (Isaiah 11:1–9). The Targum names the Messiah in both, and Qumran texts read chapter 11 of the Branch of David. Many critical scholars read the poems first as hopes for a king of Isaiah's day, such as Hezekiah, or for the restored dynasty. The New Testament applies them to Jesus (Matthew 4:13–16; Romans 15:12; Revelation 5:5).
sections.refs: Isaiah 9:1–7; Isaiah 11:1–10; Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 4:13–16; Luke 1:32–33; Romans 15:12; Revelation 5:5; Revelation 22:16

sections.h: Shear-jashub and the remnant in Isaiah 7–11
sections.b: Isaiah named his son Shear-jashub, "a remnant will return" (Isaiah 7:3). The name is two-edged: only a remnant, and yet a remnant. Isaiah 10:20–23 explains it. The survivors of Israel will stop leaning on the empire that beat them and lean on the LORD; "A remnant will return, Jacob's remnant, to the Mighty God" (Isaiah 10:21); but though Israel were like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return. In 11:11–16 the LORD gathers that remnant from Assyria, Egypt and the ends of the earth on a highway home. Paul quotes the Greek of 10:22–23 to say that God has always kept a remnant within Israel (Romans 9:27–28).

Isaiah 11:2 promises that "The LORD's Spirit will come to rest on him", the shoot of Jesse, with three pairs of gifts: wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and the fear of the LORD. The Spirit had come on Israel's judges and on David at his anointing (1 Samuel 16:13); here the Spirit rests, a lasting gift. The Greek and Latin versions list seven, which the church came to call the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The Gospels show the Spirit coming down on Jesus at his baptism and staying on him (John 1:32–33), and Isaiah 61:1 takes up the theme again: the Spirit of the Lord GOD is on the anointed messenger.
sections.refs: Isaiah 11:2–3; 1 Samuel 16:13; Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 61:1; Matthew 3:16; John 1:32–33; Luke 4:18

sections.b: The crisis of Isaiah 7 is a crisis of the promise to David: Aram and Israel plan to put a stranger on Judah's throne. Isaiah addresses "the house of David" (Isaiah 7:2, 13), and his word "you will not be held firm" (Isaiah 7:9) plays on the promise that David's house and kingdom "will be made secure forever" (2 Samuel 7:16, where the Hebrew uses the same root). The hope of 9:7 is a king "on David's throne and over his kingdom" whose rule has no end, and 11:1 goes back past David to Jesse, as if the dynasty had to sprout again from the roots. Isaiah holds together judgment on unfaithful kings and confidence that God will keep his word to David.
sections.refs: Isaiah 7:2; Isaiah 7:9; Isaiah 7:13; Isaiah 9:7; Isaiah 11:1; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 89:3–4

sections.b: Isaiah 7–10 is written in the shadow of Tiglath-pileser III and his successors. Ahaz hires Assyria against Aram and Israel, and Isaiah warns that the hired razor will shave Judah too (Isaiah 7:20). Assyria is the flood of the River up to Judah's neck (Isaiah 8:7–8), and "the rod of my anger" (Isaiah 10:5), sent by the LORD against a godless nation. But the Assyrian king boasts that he did it all himself and that Jerusalem's God is like the idols of the cities he took (Isaiah 10:8–14). The LORD will judge him as a tool that boasts against its user (Isaiah 10:15). Peter Machinist has shown how closely these speeches mirror Assyria's royal inscriptions.
sections.refs: Isaiah 7:17–20; Isaiah 8:7–8; Isaiah 10:5–19; Isaiah 10:24–34; 2 Kings 16:7–9; 2 Kings 18:13

sections.h: Isaiah 10: the ax and the one who swings it
sections.b: Isaiah 10:5–15 is one of the Bible's clearest statements of how God works through human powers. The LORD sends Assyria to punish, but "he does not see it that way" (Isaiah 10:7): the king of Assyria intends conquest for its own sake. God's purpose and the king's purpose run side by side, and the king is judged for his pride and cruelty. "Can an ax take credit over the man who chops with it?" (Isaiah 10:15). The same pattern appears in Joseph's words to his brothers (Genesis 50:20) and in Acts 4:27–28. Isaiah draws from it both comfort for the oppressed and a warning to every power that thinks it acts alone.

Isaiah 9:1 names "the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali", "the way of the sea, the far side of the Jordan, Galilee of the nations": the northern regions Assyria took from Israel in 733–732 BC (2 Kings 15:29). The land first humbled would be first honored, and its people, walking in the dark, would see a great light (Isaiah 9:2). Matthew 4:13–16 quotes the passage when Jesus moves to Capernaum "in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali". "Galilee of the nations" (galil haggoyim, "the district of the nations") reflects a region where many non-Israelites lived, which Matthew may have heard as a hint of the gospel going to the Gentiles.

Isaiah 11:6–9 is a central text in debates over the millennium. Wolf and lamb, leopard and goat, lion and calf live together, and a child plays at a cobra's hole, because "knowing the LORD will fill the earth" (Isaiah 11:9). Irenaeus read it literally of the kingdom on a renewed earth; premillennial and dispensational Christians place it in Christ's thousand-year reign; amillennial readers place it on the new earth or read it of the gospel's peace; Maimonides read it as a parable of Israel living safely among the nations. Isaiah 65:25 repeats the scene within the promise of new heavens and a new earth.

"You will draw water with joy / out of the springs of rescue" (Isaiah 12:3) has long been tied to the water libation of the Feast of Booths. Each morning of the feast a priest drew water from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and poured it on the altar, and the nights were given to torchlit celebration: whoever had not seen "the joy of the water-drawing", the Mishnah says, had never seen joy (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9–5:1). On the last day of that feast Jesus called out, "If anyone is thirsty, he should come to me and drink" (John 7:37).

Isaiah 10–12 retells the hope of rescue in exodus terms. The LORD will lift his staff over the sea "the way it was done in Egypt" (Isaiah 10:26). He will reach out "a second time" to claim his people as his own (Isaiah 11:11), split the tongue of Egypt's sea and the River so that people cross in sandals (Isaiah 11:15), and make a road for the remnant "like the road Israel had / on the day it came up out of the land of Egypt" (Isaiah 11:16). Then the people sing, as Moses and Israel sang, "my strength and my song is Yah, the LORD" (Isaiah 12:2; Exodus 15:2). Chapters 40–55 take the theme much further.

sections.b: In chapters 7–8 the prophet's family is part of his message. He takes his son Shear-jashub, "a remnant will return", to meet Ahaz (Isaiah 7:3); he writes the name Maher-shalal-hash-baz, "quick to the plunder", on a public tablet and then gives it to the son born to him and "the prophetess", his wife (Isaiah 8:1–4). "Look at me and the children the LORD has given me: / we are signs and omens in Israel" (Isaiah 8:18). Rejected by the king, Isaiah seals his teaching among his disciples and waits for the LORD (Isaiah 8:16–17), the first glimpse of the circle that kept his words.

Isaiah 8:19 mocks those who advise, "Consult the ghosts of the dead and the spirits that know things, who chirp and mutter." The words 'ov and yidde'oni are the ones the law forbids (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:11) and the ones used of the medium at Endor (1 Samuel 28:7–9). Isaiah's answer is short: a people should consult its own God, not go to the dead about the living, and turn "Back to the teaching and the witness!" (Isaiah 8:20).
